clue.text: Inattentive pedestrian perhaps crosses end of avenue

indicators.note: the car-free word stretches across the single letter, holding it inside

parts.note: a pedestrian is, for example, someone car-less, going on foot

indicators.note: the last letter of the word avenue is taken

parts.note: supplies its final letter

explanation.surface: A distracted walker strays across the end of a tree-lined avenue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pedestrian' looks like the word meaning dull, but 'perhaps' marks it as an example: a walker is someone without a car.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone careless is not paying proper attention, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: It can transport a large number

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a floating platform that carries people or goods on water
second meaning: as in 'a ... of measures', a great many

explanation.walkthrough: CART also carries things, but 'a cart of' is not a phrase for a large number; only the floating platform gives both senses.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names a flat floating craft and, idiomatically, a big collection of things, as in 'a raft of changes'.

clue.text: Thick unpleasant smell above climber

indicators.note: in a down entry the first piece sits on top of the second

parts.note: BO is body odour, an unpleasant smell
a vine is a climbing plant

explanation.surface: A dense, nasty smell hangs over a climbing plant in the garden.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Thick' means stupid here, not dense in texture.
explanation.definitionFit: Cow-like dullness: someone bovine is slow-witted, the same informal sense as thick meaning stupid.

clue.text: Powerless to cross street to get bananas

indicators.note: the word for powerless lies across the abbreviation, so it ends up enclosing it

parts.note: unable means lacking the power to do something

explanation.surface: Someone too weak to cross the road to fetch some fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like the fruit being fetched, but it is the slang definition: crazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Going bananas is slang for going mad, and an unstable person is mentally unbalanced.

clue.text: Directories head of department lost when moving desk

indicators.note: the letter at the head of department is dropped from the fodder before the rearranging
the remaining letters move around into a new order
the first letter of the word department is taken

parts.note: supplies its initial letter

explanation.surface: An office reorganisation: phone directories go missing when the head of department moves desks.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the D (head of department) out of DIRECTORIES, and the remaining ten letters, IRECTORIES, rearrange to give the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: An escritoire is a writing desk with drawers and a hinged writing surface.

clue.text: Locks securing books and eyewash

indicators.note: the hair holds the books inside it, as if keeping them safe

parts.note: locks of hair
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Hair grips hold books in place, plus a mention of eye lotion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Eyewash' is not a lotion here but the informal word for nonsense.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are informal words for empty, pretentious talk or nonsense meant to impress.

clue.text: Highly suspicious airman lacking papers

parts.note: a para is a paratrooper, a soldier who arrives by air
with no ID, identity papers: NO ID

explanation.surface: A pilot without identity documents arouses deep suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: A para is a parachute soldier, here loosely an airman.
explanation.definitionFit: A paranoid person is irrationally distrustful, extremely suspicious of others.

clue.text: Failure in half of London area?

parts.note: demi- is a prefix meaning half
SE is a London postal district, south-east London

explanation.surface: A question of whether a collapse happened in half of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half of London area' reads as one phrase, but 'half' is DEMI and 'London area' is SE, a London postcode area.
explanation.definitionFit: A demise is an end or downfall, the collapse of a business or plan, so it means failure.

clue.text: Son who plays truant

indicators.note: the letters play about, rearranging themselves into a new word

explanation.surface: A boy who skips school.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plays' seems to belong with 'truant' as in 'plays truant', but it is the anagram signal on SON WHO.
explanation.definitionFit: A no-show is a person who fails to turn up when expected, as a truant fails to attend school.

clue.text: Relish is French with zero added

indicators.note: with ... added says the pieces are joined together

parts.note: Z is listed in Chambers as an abbreviation for zero, as in ZPG (zero population growth)
est is French for 'is'

explanation.surface: A remark that relish is French, with a zero tacked on.
explanation.walkthrough: Z for zero is a rare abbreviation, found in dictionaries mostly in compounds like ZPG.
explanation.definitionFit: Zest is keen enjoyment or enthusiasm, the same as relish in 'eat with relish'.

clue.text: Irrelevant alarm I time to go off

indicators.note: the letters go off in a new arrangement, as an alarm going off is set in motion

explanation.surface: A dismissive shrug: it doesn't matter when my alarm is set to ring.
explanation.definitionFit: Something immaterial is unimportant or beside the point, of no consequence to the matter.

clue.text: Threat from soldiers on crack

indicators.note: the first piece goes next to the second

parts.note: men is a common word for soldiers
crack as an adjective means expert, an ace

explanation.surface: A danger posed by soldiers taking drugs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crack' looks like the drug, but it means first-class, as in a crack shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A menace is a person or thing likely to cause harm, a danger or threat.

clue.text: Questionable royal chap dancing around front of palace

indicators.note: the jumbled letters go round the single letter, enclosing it
the letters dance about into a new order
the first letter of the word palace is taken

parts.note: supplies its first letter

explanation.surface: A dubious story about a royal man dancing in front of the palace.
explanation.walkthrough: ROYALCHAP rearranges to APOCRYHAL, which goes around P (front of palace).
explanation.definitionFit: An apocryphal story is of doubtful authenticity, widely told but probably untrue.

clue.text: Pitiful tale of son of a bitch and Southern politician

parts.note: SOB is the abbreviation of son of a bitch
a Tory is a British Conservative politician

explanation.surface: A tragic story about a scoundrel and a Conservative from the south.
explanation.walkthrough: A Tory is a member of Britain's Conservative Party.
explanation.definitionFit: A sob story is a tale of woe told to win sympathy, a pitiful account.

clue.text: Throw about rum that's cheap and nasty

indicators.note: the throw word goes about the strange word, enclosing it

parts.note: to shy is to throw, as at a coconut shy
rum in British use means strange or odd

explanation.surface: Tossing some rum around that tastes cheap and nasty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' is the old British adjective for strange, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Shoddy goods are badly made from inferior materials, poor quality at a low price.

clue.text: Good government has merely to disregard outsiders and follow party lines

indicators.note: the following pieces come after the party word

parts.note: a do is a party or celebration

indicators.note: drop the outer letters of the word merely and keep its inside

explanation.surface: A political slogan: good government means merely ignoring outsiders and toeing the party line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'party lines' looks like one political phrase; 'party' is DO and 'lines' is the definition. EREL is merely without its outside letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Doggerel is comic or badly written verse, so lines of poor poetry.

clue.text: Use gin to develop brilliance

indicators.note: the letters develop into another form, a reworking of their order

explanation.surface: Advice that drinking gin will help bring out brilliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Genius is exceptional intellectual or creative ability, which is what brilliance means here.

clue.text: Consignment from small trendy chaps with a bit of talent

parts.note: hip means fashionable or trendy
men, chaps

indicators.note: only a small part, the first letter, of the word talent is used

parts.note: supplies its first letter

explanation.surface: A delivery of short, fashionable men with a touch of talent.
explanation.definitionFit: A shipment is a quantity of goods sent together, which is what a consignment is.

clue.text: Iron crease for Tom perhaps

parts.note: Fe is the chemical symbol for iron
a line is a crease or wrinkle

explanation.surface: Ironing out a crease for someone called Tom.
explanation.walkthrough: Tom is not a man's name here but a male cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A tom is a male cat, an example of a member of the cat family.

clue.text: Suspend meetings of professional fraudster?

parts.note: pro is short for professional
a rogue is a dishonest person, a swindler

explanation.surface: Asking whether a career con man would put a stop to meetings.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the long phrase at the start, the parliamentary sense.
explanation.definitionFit: To prorogue a parliament is to discontinue its sessions without dissolving it.

clue.text: King in dodgy rodeo cheated

indicators.note: the king letter goes inside the jumbled letters
dodgy suggests something unreliable or crooked, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

explanation.surface: A king was swindled at a crooked rodeo.
explanation.walkthrough: RODEO rearranges to ROOED, with K inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To rook someone is old slang for swindling them out of money.

clue.text: Small, almost entirely disgusting, bug

parts.note: wee is Scottish and informal for small

indicators.note: all but the last letter of the word is kept

parts.note: vile means disgusting

explanation.surface: A small, nearly completely revolting insect.
explanation.definitionFit: A weevil is a small beetle, and bug is a general word for any insect.

clue.text: Secure present for fan

parts.note: to win something is to secure it
the present is now

explanation.surface: Guarantee a gift for a supporter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fan' is not a supporter but the verb for blowing chaff away from grain.
explanation.definitionFit: To winnow grain is to blow air through it to separate the chaff, which is to fan it.

clue.text: Character of intricate particle

parts.note: complex means intricate
an ion is an electrically charged particle

explanation.surface: Describing the nature of a complicated tiny particle.
explanation.definitionFit: Complexion means general nature or aspect, as in 'that puts a different complexion on it'.

clue.text: Papers initially banned under ministerial framework

indicators.note: take the first letter of each of the following words

explanation.surface: Documents first banned under a government framework.
explanation.walkthrough: Bumf is British slang for paperwork or documents.
explanation.definitionFit: Bumf is informal British slang for tedious paperwork, documents and leaflets.

clue.text: Smear something on back of book obscuring ending

indicators.note: the last letter is hidden from view, so it is dropped

parts.note: a blurb is the promotional text printed on the back of a book

explanation.surface: Smudging the text on a book jacket so its end can't be read.
explanation.definitionFit: A blur is a smudge or smear that makes something indistinct.

clue.text: Passed a territory containing grave

indicators.note: the phrase holds the answer inside its letters, running across the words

explanation.surface: Travelling through a region that holds a burial site.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grave' looks like a burial place, but it is the adjective meaning serious.
explanation.definitionFit: Sedate means calm and dignified, and Chambers gives grave in that sober, serious sense.

clue.text: Look after European that Parisian conservation group finds persuasive

indicators.note: the look word comes after the European letter

parts.note: lo is an old word for look
que is French for that
NT is the National Trust, a British heritage conservation body

explanation.surface: A conservation body in Paris looks after Europeans and wins people over.
explanation.walkthrough: The National Trust is a British charity that looks after historic houses and countryside.
explanation.definitionFit: Eloquent speech is fluent and expressive, and so moving or persuasive.
